title: The ins and outs of the DEATH TAX
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the "death tax," covering the estate tax and inheritance tax. They trace its history from ancient Egypt and Rome (the vicesima hereditatium) through medieval England and the Magna Carta, the American colonies' Stamp Act, the Civil War inheritance tax, the 1916 income-tax-era estate tax, the World War II-era 77 percent top rate, and the 2001-2013 exemption increases under the Bush tax cuts and the 2012 Taxpayer Relief Act. They also cover the gift tax and its loopholes, the generation-skipping transfer tax, arguments for and against the tax, and current exemption levels. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Ethan Barber.

segments.title: Opening banter and intro to the death tax
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about beverages and Chuck's name, then introduce the topic. They define the estate tax and inheritance tax as the two forms of death tax in the U.S. and describe how debts, executor fees, and funeral costs come off the top before taxes.

segments.title: Ancient Rome and Egypt death taxes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss ancient Egyptian papyrus describing death tax evasion and Caesar Augustus's vicesima hereditatium, a 5 percent tax on inheritances. Roman law included exemptions for close family and charitable gifts.

segments.title: Medieval England, Magna Carta and early philosophy
segments.summary: The hosts describe medieval English opposition to death taxes and a clause in the Magna Carta. They then discuss the philosophical debate, with Locke, Smith and Bentham opposing the tax and Blackstone supporting it to prevent dynasties.

segments.title: Stamp Act and American founding era
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the founders looked to European thinking. The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed printed documents, including legal papers and attorney licenses, to fund a naval war with France. Estates under fifty dollars were exempt. The tax was repealed in 1802.

segments.title: Civil War inheritance tax and gift tax loophole
segments.summary: The Civil War brought an inheritance tax on the recipients, later extended to real property. Taxpayers avoided estate tax by giving assets away before death, which prompted a federal gift tax in 1864.

segments.title: Populist movement, 1898 War Revenue Act and Teddy Roosevelt
segments.summary: Industrialization concentrated wealth and fueled a populist movement, with the hosts noting Frank L. Baum's Wizard of Oz as populist allegory. An income tax in 1894 was struck down. The War Revenue Act of 1898 added a state tax with exemptions and rates based on relationship. The tax was repealed in 1902, and Teddy Roosevelt backed a graduated inheritance tax to curb concentrated fortunes and political power.

segments.title: Revenue Act of 1916 and World War I, Great Depression gift tax
segments.summary: World War I led Congress to pass the Revenue Act of 1916, creating the modern income tax and estate tax. The estate tax exemption was fifty thousand dollars. The gift tax was reinstated to close the loophole, and the Great Depression prompted further equalization.

segments.title: Estate tax rates from World War II to 2001
segments.summary: From 1941 to 1977 the top estate tax rate was 77 percent. Congress lowered the top rate to 70 percent in 1977. The Tax Reform Act of 1976 raised the exemption from 60,000 to 120,000 dollars and introduced the generation-skipping transfer tax. Exemptions rose over the following decades.

segments.title: Bush tax cuts, 2010 repeal, and 2012 Taxpayer Relief Act
segments.summary: The exemption climbed to 675,000 dollars in 2009 and 3.5 million in 2009 under the Bush tax cuts, with the tax briefly absent in 2010. The 2012 Taxpayer Relief Act set the exemption at 5 million dollars, indexed for inflation, with a 40 percent top rate. The hosts explain how the unified credit works, and the annual gift exclusion of 14,000 dollars per person.

segments.title: Pros and cons of the estate tax
segments.summary: Opponents argue the tax stifles investment, punishes success, double-taxes wealth, and harms family farms and small businesses. Supporters cite a 2013 Brookings Tax Policy Institute study that found small farms and businesses paid an average of about 4.9 percent, and that the tax affects about two-tenths of one percent of households. They also argue it reduces concentrated power and that it collects roughly two billion dollars a year.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a brief remark about taxes and sign off with the usual call to action for contact channels.
